content_voiceover: This table classifies inherited platelet disorders by the specific platelet component that is abnormal, which is a really useful framework for boards because it links mechanism directly to disease name. Abnormalities of the platelet receptors for adhesive proteins involve the GPIb IX V complex, causing Bernard Soulier syndrome and platelet type von Willebrand disease, or GPIIb IIIa, also written alpha IIb beta three, causing Glanzmann thrombasthenia, these two are highlighted because they are the most testable. Abnormalities of receptors for soluble agonists involve P2Y12 or thromboxane A2 receptors, causing the respective receptor deficiencies. Abnormalities of platelet granules are split into delta granule problems, which include nonsyndromic delta storage pool deficiency, Hermansky Pudlak syndrome, and Chediak Higashi syndrome, and alpha granule problems, which include gray platelet syndrome and several rarer entities. Further down, defects of signal transduction, abnormalities of membrane phospholipids like Scott syndrome, and miscellaneous causes round out the classification. The two red underlined rows, Bernard Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, and Chediak Higashi syndrome, are emphasized because they are the highest yield for exam purposes.
keypoints: Classification is organized by which platelet component is abnormal
GPIb IX V complex defect causes Bernard Soulier syndrome
GPIIb IIIa defect causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia
Delta granule defects include Hermansky Pudlak and Chediak Higashi syndromes
Alpha granule defect is exemplified by gray platelet syndrome
keypoint_voiceover: Anchor this table to two receptor defects. GPIb IX V complex deficiency gives you Bernard Soulier syndrome, and GPIIb IIIa deficiency gives you Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Then remember delta granule defects like Chediak Higashi and Hermansky Pudlak, and alpha granule defect meaning gray platelet syndrome.
